# From Devanagari to canonical spelling: the journey of Candra

Long before it became a ​digital address, this name travelled through scripts. **Candra** begins in Devanagari, passes through scholarly transliteration, and arrives in a Latin form that needs no special encoding. Each stage ‌preserves some information and requires some judgment. This post follows that journey: the original evidence, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material remains, and the reviewed spelling ‌used by the temple.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Candra
- **ASCII form:** chandra
- **Meaning:** "Glittering, shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma ​in his lunar aspect."
- **Domain of influence:** Moon, Night, Soma
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** चन्द्र (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Candra** (*chandra*) — The Glittering Moon · Glittering, ​shining — the moon personified as a god — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Moon, Night, Soma". The name means "Glittering, ​shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in his lunar aspect.".

**Candra** is the moon personified: the glittering lord whose waxing and ​waning marks the calendar, whose crescent crowns Śiva’s hair, and whose dynasty — the Candravamśa — produced, by epic genealogy, the Pāṇḍavas and Krishna himself. In the Veda he ​is Soma’s celestial body; in later mythology he is the beautiful, cursed, forever-waning god.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Candra** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/chandra/). ‌The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *chandra* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special ​encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **चन्द्र**. Etymologically it means "Glittering, ​shining — the moon personified as a god; also a name of Soma in his lunar aspect.".

The canonical spelling **Candra** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ‌ASCII form *chandra* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization ​and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **चन्द्र**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Candra*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit ‌Candra is written in Devanagari as चन्द्र
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath ​consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈtʃʌndrə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Candra).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **C-** — In IAST, ​c is the English “ch” — palatal, never a k-sound.
- **-an-** — Short a as in “cup”; the syllable is light.
- **-dra** — The cluster dr; the name ​means “glittering, shining”. In Vedic the moon is more often Soma.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “CHUN-druh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Vedic** ​— Soma — the moon as the soma-plant’s celestial home
- **Greek** — Men, the lunar god of the Anatolian coast

The lunar dynasty of the epics — the ​Candravamśa — traces every lunar king to him.

## Mythology

Candra’s mythology clusters around two stories: the theft of Tārā and its curse, and the moon-churning of the ocean ‌of milk. He is the most beautiful of the gods and the most diminished — the waxing and waning written into his body as punishment and mercy at once.

### ​The Abduction of Tārā (Purāṇic Cycle)

Candra loved Tārā, wife of the guru Bṛhaspati, and carried her off; the gods’ war over her ended with her return — ‌and her pregnancy, which she refused to explain until the child’s radiance declared the moon his father. Budha, the child, founded the lunar dynasty through which the epic’s ​heroes descend.

### The Curse and the Mercy (Śiva Cycle)

Dakṣa, Bṛhaspati’s champion, cursed the moon to waste to nothing; the pleading gods won a partial reprieve — the ‌curse would lift for half each month. The phases of the moon are the scar of the love-affair, and Śiva’s wearing of the crescent is the war-god’s mercy ​made ornament.

### The Moon from the Churning (Samudra Manthana)

When the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, the moon rose among ‌the treasures — Dhanvantari’s medicine-chest, the apsarases, and Candra, the glittering disc. Śiva took him onto his brow; the poison of the churning, Halāhala, he drank instead, turning ​his throat blue.

### The Celestial Plant (Vedic Soma)

In the Veda the moon is Soma’s home: the pressed plant’s juice ascends to become the lunar disc, and the moon’s ‌quarters are the soma-cup’s refills. The identification of moon, plant, and god is the Veda’s most compact theology — three substances, one divinity.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography ​associated with Candra concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Waxing Fortnight** — The bright half of the month, ​śuklapakṣa, is his growth — the calendar’s first engine.
- **Śiva’s Diadem** — The crescent moon in Śiva’s hair is Candra’s seat — cooled by the Ganges, crowned by ‌it.
- **Father of Budha** — By Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati, he fathered Budha — Mercury and ancestor of the lunar line.
- **The Waning Curse** — Cursed by Dakṣa ‌to waste away for loving Tārā, he is saved by Śiva’s partial mercy — hence the phases.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Candra survives in a ‌small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Candra rides the ​temple friezes as the lunar graha; the great crescents of the medieval Śiva temples of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are his monumental form. The astronomical observatories of Jantar ​Mantar measure his cycles in stone.

## Realm & Domain

**Candra** is the moon personified: the glittering lord whose waxing and waning marks the calendar, whose crescent crowns Śiva’s hair, ‌and whose dynasty — the Candravamśa — produced, by epic genealogy, the Pāṇḍavas and Krishna himself. In the Veda he is Soma’s celestial body; in later mythology he ​is the beautiful, cursed, forever-waning god.

### The Waxing Fortnight

The bright half of the month, śuklapakṣa, is his growth — the calendar’s first engine.

### Śiva’s Diadem

The crescent ​moon in Śiva’s hair is Candra’s seat — cooled by the Ganges, crowned by it.

### Father of Budha

By Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati, he fathered Budha — Mercury ‌and ancestor of the lunar line.

### The Waning Curse

Cursed by Dakṣa to waste away for loving Tārā, he is saved by Śiva’s partial mercy — hence the ​phases.

## Across Cultures

Candra fused with Soma in the Vedic period and with the astronomical moon (one of the nine grahas) in the medieval period. The Greeks of ​the Northwest compared him to Selene’s domain but found no single Olympian match; and the Buddhist lunar mansions (nakṣatras) kept his calendar alive across Asia.

Kindred figures in ‌the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[artemis|Ártemis]], [[change|Chángé]], [[hati|Hati]], [[hekate|Hekátē]], [[mamaquilla|Mama Quilla]], and [[mani|Máni]], each linked through moon / lunar.

## Cultural Legacy

The lunar calendar — every Hindu festival’s dating ​— is his monument; the Candravamśa genealogy made him the ancestor of the epic’s heroes. The crescent in Śiva’s hair is Hinduism’s most reproduced ornament; and ‘Monday’ (somavāra) ‌still speaks his Vedic name in every Indian week.

## A Meditation

Candra: the glittering one, restored in plain letters that glitter on the screen. His waxing ​and waning need no diacritic — the phases are written in the name’s rhythm, two syllables that fill and empty like the moon they name.

The plain ASCII form *chandra* contains the same letters, so there are no lost diacritics to recover and no ‌special encoding transition to explain. ## A Closer Look at the Spelling

A canonical name is a small map. In the ​case of **Candra**, the route does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the conventional scholarly spelling already uses the Latin alphabet. The original evidence — **चन्द्र** ‌in Devanagari — carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce.

By fixing one reviewed spelling as the public reference, the project prevents the drift ​that occurs when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The character list shows exactly what is carried forward. "No change" here means a ​deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and faithful to the record.
